subcards.title: Prime Minister (Art 75, 78)
subcards.summary: How the PM is appointed, what the PM does, and who has held the post.
at_a_glance: 74 (Council headed by PM), 75 (appointment), 78 (PM's duties to President)
President (Art 75(1)) – leader who has Lok Sabha majority
Real (de facto) executive; head of government. President = head of State
Either House; a non-member can be PM for 6 months
Not fixed – holds office while Lok Sabha majority supports
Office and secrecy, given by the President

Narendra Modi – 14th PM, in office since 26 May 2014; 3rd term from 9 June 2024 (as of Nov 2026)

blocks.title: Appointment (Art 75(1))
items: The Constitution gives no special procedure for choosing the PM. Art 75 says only that the President appoints the Prime Minister (PM). The other ministers are appointed by the President on the PM's advice.
By convention (an accepted practice, not written law), the President must appoint the leader of the party that has a majority in the Lok Sabha.

In a hung House (no party has a clear majority), the President uses personal discretion (own judgement). He usually appoints the leader of the largest party or coalition and asks that person to win a vote of confidence (floor test – a vote in the Lok Sabha) within a month.
This discretion was first used in 1979: President Neelam Sanjiva Reddy appointed Charan Singh (leader of a coalition) after Morarji Desai's Janata government fell.

The second situation for discretion is the sudden death of a PM with no obvious successor. In 1984, after Indira Gandhi's assassination, President Zail Singh appointed Rajiv Gandhi directly. He did not follow the earlier practice of first appointing a caretaker (temporary) PM.
If the ruling party elects a new leader after the PM's death, the President has no choice: he must appoint that leader as PM.

Delhi High Court (1980): a person need not prove a Lok Sabha majority before being appointed PM. The President may appoint first and then ask the PM to prove the majority within a reasonable time. PMs appointed this way: Charan Singh (1979), V.P. Singh (1989), Chandra Shekhar (1990), P.V. Narasimha Rao (1991), Vajpayee (1996 and 1998), Deve Gowda (1996), I.K. Gujral (1997).
The first PM (Nehru, 1947) was appointed by the Governor-General, Lord Mountbatten, because India had no President until 26 Jan 1950.

blocks.title: Membership of Parliament
head: Point
Rule
rows: The PM may be a member of either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha
Can be appointed PM for 6 months; must become a member of either House within that time, else ceases to be PM – S.P. Anand v. H.D. Deve Gowda (Supreme Court, decided 6 Nov 1996; reported 1997)
Art 75(5): any minister who is not a Member of Parliament (MP) for 6 months in a row stops being a minister (details in the Council of Ministers card)
The Constitution does not stop a nominated MP from becoming a Union minister
Laxmikanth names three: Indira Gandhi (1966), H.D. Deve Gowda (1996), Manmohan Singh (2004). I.K. Gujral (1997) was also a Rajya Sabha member (from Bihar) when appointed
Can speak in the Lok Sabha (Art 88) but cannot VOTE there – not even on a no-confidence motion against his/her own government

If the PM is a Lok Sabha member, the PM is the Leader of the House (Lok Sabha). If not, the PM nominates a minister who is a Lok Sabha member. Example: in the 14th Lok Sabha (2004–09) Manmohan Singh was in the Rajya Sabha, so Pranab Mukherjee was Leader of the House
In Britain the PM must be a member of the Lower House (House of Commons)

blocks.title: Oath, term, salary
head: Item
Details
rows: Given by the President. Swears: (1) true faith and allegiance to the Constitution, (2) uphold sovereignty and integrity of India, (3) faithfully discharge duties, (4) do right to all people without fear or favour, affection or ill will
Will not reveal any matter that comes to him/her as a Union minister, except as needed for duties. Same form as any Union minister

Not fixed; holds office 'during the pleasure of the President' – in practice, as long as the Lok Sabha majority supports. Cannot be dismissed while majority lasts; on losing confidence must resign or President can dismiss (e.g. V.P. Singh 1990 and Deve Gowda 1997 resigned after losing a confidence vote)

Decided by Parliament (NOT the President) – Salaries and Allowances of Ministers Act, 1952. Gets an MP's salary plus a sumptuary allowance (allowance for official hospitality; raised from ₹1,500 to ₹3,000/month in 2001), free house, travel, medical
SPG (Special Protection Group) (Amendment) Act, 2019: sitting PM and family living with him get SPG cover; a former PM and family get it only for 5 years after leaving office

blocks.text: Deputy Prime Minister: not mentioned in the Constitution. Devi Lal case (1990): Supreme Court said the title is only descriptive and gives no powers of the PM; holder is just a minister. Appointed mostly for political reasons.

blocks.title: Powers and functions
head: In relation to
Powers
rows: Recommends persons to be appointed ministers (President can appoint only those the PM recommends – the ONLY PM power written in the Constitution, Art 75(1)); allocates and reshuffles portfolios (formally done by the President on PM's advice under business rules); can ask a minister to resign or advise President to dismiss him; presides over meetings; guides and coordinates all ministers; can collapse the whole Council by resigning

Principal channel of communication between President and Council of Ministers (Art 78); advises appointment of Attorney General, CAG (Comptroller and Auditor General), UPSC chairman and members, Election Commissioners, Finance Commission chairman and members, etc.

Leader of the Lower House; advises President on summoning and proroguing (ending a session) Parliament; can recommend dissolution of Lok Sabha at any time (Art 85 – no emergency needed); announces government policy on the floor

Chairman of NITI Aayog (successor of Planning Commission), National Integration Council, Inter-State Council, National Water Resources Council; shapes foreign policy; chief spokesman of the Union government; crisis manager-in-chief in emergencies; leader of the nation and of the ruling party; political head of the services

blocks.title: Art 78 – duties of the PM towards the President
items: (a) Communicate to the President ALL decisions of the Council of Ministers on Union administration and proposals for legislation.
(b) Furnish information on Union administration and legislative proposals that the President calls for.
(c) If the President requires, submit for the Council's consideration any matter decided by a single minister but not considered by the Council.

blocks.text: Death or resignation of the PM automatically dissolves the whole Council of Ministers (because the Council has the PM 'at the head' – Art 74). Death or resignation of any other minister only creates a vacancy.

blocks.title: Order of first taking office (sequence questions)
Caretaker government
items: No provision in the Constitution – a convention and 'functional necessity', not a separate office.
Means: a Council of Ministers that has resigned (lost confidence, or Lok Sabha dissolved) but is asked by the President to continue until a new government takes office – avoids a vacuum.
Role limited to routine work; no major new policies, projects or spending, except for national security or national interest.

Tarkunde Committee (1974–75, unofficial 'JP Committee' on electoral reforms): caretaker should not announce new policies, start new projects, give loans or salary increases, or hold official functions with ministers.
Calcutta High Court (Dec 1979): only day-to-day administration allowed.

items: Executive action is taken in the name of the PRESIDENT (Art 77), not the PM.

Salary of the PM and ministers is decided by Parliament, not President.

subcards.title: Council of Ministers (Art 74, 75, 77)
subcards.summary: Who advises the President, how ministers are appointed, and to whom they answer.
at_a_glance: At most 15% of Lok Sabha strength, counting the PM — 91st Amendment, 2003
A non-member can stay minister for at most 6 months in a row
Made binding by 42nd Amendment (1976); President can return it once for reconsideration — 44th Amendment (1978)

blocks.text: India has a parliamentary system: the President is the nominal (de jure) head; the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister is the real (de facto) executive. Articles 74 and 75 set this up only in a broad, sketchy way.

blocks.title: Article 74 in two clauses
head: Clause
What it says
Added/changed by
rows: There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President, who shall act in accordance with such advice
'shall act in accordance' made explicit by 42nd Amendment (1976)
President may send the advice back ONCE for reconsideration; after reconsideration he must act on it
The advice tendered by ministers to the President shall not be inquired into in any court

steps.detail: may repeat the same advice unchanged

steps.step: President must act on the re-tendered advice

blocks.title: Key points
items: 42nd Amendment (1976) — FIRST made the advice obligatory (binding) on the President.
44th Amendment (1978) — added the one-time reconsideration; this is the PRESENT position.

Exact position (for statement questions): the 42nd Amendment (1976) made advice binding; the 44th Amendment (1978) kept it binding and only added one return for reconsideration. So a President who refuses binding advice violates the Constitution and may face impeachment — except in marginal cases of situational discretion recognised by the Supreme Court. Crediting the binding rule itself to the 44th is loose wording.
Refusing binding advice = acting against the Constitution, which can be a ground for impeachment (except marginal cases of situational discretion the Supreme Court recognised).
A Council of Ministers must ALWAYS exist — even after Lok Sabha dissolution or the PM's resignation (outgoing ministry continues as caretaker).
Even during a National Emergency the President gets NO personal discretion — he still acts on ministers' advice.
Early dissolution of Lok Sabha: President acts under Art 85 on the advice of a majority-backed Council (Art 74); no Emergency needed. PM himself does not issue the order.
Art 74(2) stops courts from asking WHETHER advice was given and WHAT it was — it does not protect every executive order from courts.

Both PM (Lok Sabha) and CM (Assembly) can advise dissolution of their Lower House. President's Rule (Art 356) is not 'only on the PM's recommendation' — it follows the Governor's report or other information, acted on with Union ministerial advice.

Terms: nominal executive is the President; real executive is the Council of Ministers headed by the PM; shadow cabinet is the opposition's team that mirrors the ruling cabinet (a British practice, not in Indian law).

A ministry that has resigned (or after dissolution) is asked by the President to continue till a successor takes office — a convention to avoid a vacuum; it handles only routine work, no major new policies (Tarkunde Committee 1974-75; Calcutta High Court 1979).

blocks.title: Appointment & membership
items: Ministers are usually MPs of either House; a non-member can be a minister for 6 months — and even PM (S.P. Anand case).
A nominated member of either House can be a minister — no constitutional bar.
Constitution does NOT require Cabinet ministers (or the Finance Minister) to be Lok Sabha members — a Rajya Sabha member can be a minister, even PM.
The PM has full discretion in choosing ministers; the President only formally appoints them.
Giving every region and state a place in the ministry is a convention (practice), not a constitutional rule.

Oath of office: bear true faith to the Constitution, uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India, do his duties faithfully, and do right to all people without fear or favour. Oath of secrecy: not reveal any matter that comes before him as a minister, except as his duty requires.

Salary: same as an MP, plus a sumptuary allowance (allowance for hospitality expenses) by rank, free housing, travel and medical facilities. Sumptuary allowance from 2001: PM ₹3,000, Cabinet minister ₹2,000, Minister of State ₹1,000, Deputy Minister ₹600 per month.

blocks.text: see Prime Minister — appointment of PM, Art 78 duties

blocks.title: 91st Amendment Act, 2003
head: Provision
Where
rows: Union ministers, counting the PM, cannot exceed 15% of Lok Sabha strength
State ministers, counting the CM, cannot exceed 15% of Assembly strength — but cannot be fewer than 12
An MP disqualified for defection cannot be made a minister
An MLA or MLC disqualified for defection cannot be made a minister
Defector barred from any remunerative political post
Removed the 'split' exemption (earlier, if one-third of a party's legislators broke away it was not treated as defection)

items: Example: an Assembly of 60 members — 15% is 9, but the minimum is 12, so it can have 12 ministers.
NCRWC (2002) had recommended a stricter 10% ceiling; Parliament adopted 15%.
Background: coalition governments had very large ministries ('Jumbo Ministry') — the A.B. Vajpayee ministry of 1999 had more than 70 ministers.
The 91st Amendment did NOT fix 12 as the maximum size of a state ministry — 12 is the MINIMUM.

blocks.text: The Constitution does NOT classify ministers into ranks. The three-tier pattern comes from British convention; the Salaries and Allowances of Ministers Act 1952 defines 'minister' to include a deputy minister.

head: Category
Role
Cabinet meetings?
rows: Head important ministries (Home, Defence, Finance, External Affairs)
Members of the Cabinet; attend all its meetings
Run their own ministry or department, with the same powers as a Cabinet minister there
Not members of the Cabinet; attend only when invited because their subject is discussed
Work under a Cabinet minister — given some departments or items of work of his ministry
Have no ministry of their own; help Cabinet ministers or Ministers of State in administrative, political and parliamentary work
Attached to senior ministers to help with parliamentary duties; hold no department
NOT part of the Council of Ministers; appointed by the PM, not the President

items: Order of rank (by practice, not by the Constitution): from top to bottom — PM, Cabinet minister, Minister of State with independent charge, Minister of State, Deputy Minister — a Deputy Minister is BELOW a Minister of State.
Ministers are NOT all equal — rank, pay and political importance differ.
A Deputy PM is appointed mostly for political reasons; descriptive title only.

blocks.title: Three kinds of responsibility
head: Aspect
Collective
Individual
Legal
rows: All ministers 'swim or sink together': if the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, the whole ministry resigns — including ministers who are Rajya Sabha members
The President (on the PM's advice) can remove a single minister even when the ministry still has the Lok Sabha's confidence
No legal responsibility: a President's order need not be countersigned (signed again) by a minister, unlike Britain; and courts cannot inquire into ministers' advice

blocks.title: Collective responsibility explained
items: Fundamental principle of parliamentary government; also why India is called parliamentary.
Cabinet decisions bind every minister even if he disagreed in the meeting — must defend them inside and outside Parliament, or resign (cabinet solidarity).
Resignations: Dr B.R. Ambedkar (Hindu Code Bill), C.D. Deshmukh (states reorganisation), Arif Mohammed Khan (Muslim Women Act 1986).
Applies to coalition ministries too — a common programme gives the policy basis.

Rajya Sabha cannot remove the ministry because Art 75(3) makes it responsible only to the Lok Sabha (not because Rajya Sabha members are indirectly elected by MLAs) — hence the two Houses are not co-equal; Lok Sabha also prevails on Money Bills.
A ministry that loses Lok Sabha confidence may instead advise dissolution; the President need not accept it.
Resignation or death of the PM ends the whole Council (he is its head); a single minister leaving does not.

blocks.title: Individual responsibility
items: President removes a minister only on the PM's advice; the PM cannot dismiss a minister himself — he asks him to resign or advises the President.
Ambedkar: collective responsibility can be achieved only through the instrumentality of the PM.

blocks.title: No-confidence vs censure motion (Lok Sabha only)
head: Aspect
No-confidence motion
Censure motion
rows: Not mentioned — it comes from Rule 198 of the Lok Sabha Rules of Procedure
Individual minister, a group, or whole Council
Admission (allowing it to be taken up)
Speaker decides whether to admit it; at least 50 members must support it

blocks.title: Parliament's other controls
items: Parliament also controls the ministry through Question Hour, supplementary questions, adjournment motions, calling-attention motions, confidence motions and debates.

blocks.title: Article 77 — conduct of business
head: Clause
Provision
rows: All executive action of the Government of India is expressed to be taken in the name of the PRESIDENT (not the PM)
Orders authenticated as per rules made by the President; an authenticated order cannot be questioned on the ground that the President did not personally make it
President makes rules for convenient transaction of business and its allocation among ministers — Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961 and (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961

items: Ministries/departments are created and allocated to ministers by the President on the PM's advice (not by the PM on the Cabinet Secretary's advice).

Only power of the PM written in the Constitution among usual ones: advising the President on appointing ministers (Art 75(1)). Allocating portfolios, summoning Cabinet, transfers are by rules/convention.

head: Aspect
Council of Ministers
Cabinet
rows: Wider body (at most 15% of Lok Sabha strength)
Cabinet ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers
Does not meet as a body; no collective functions

head: Amendment (year)
Change

blocks.title: Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, 2025
items: Introduced in Lok Sabha on 20 August 2025 and referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC).

The PM or a Union minister (and also CMs and state ministers) would be removed if arrested and detained in custody for 30 consecutive days on an accusation of an offence punishable with 5 years or more.
Not yet enacted — on 17 July 2026 the JPC deferred adopting its draft report for more consultations; still pending (as of Nov 2026).
Collectively responsible to LOK SABHA — not Parliament, not the President.
The 15% cap counts the PM too — 91st Amendment, 2003 (NCRWC had wanted 10%). In States the minimum is 12 ministers.
A non-member gets six months IN A ROW; he cannot be reappointed again in the same term without being elected (S.R. Chaudhuri case, 2001).
Constitution does not rank ministers; parliamentary secretaries are not ministers.
Executive action in the name of the PRESIDENT (Art 77), not the PM.
The 42nd Amendment first made advice binding; the present position comes from the 44th Amendment (President can return advice once).
Ministers speak in both Houses but vote only in their own (Art 88).

subcards.summary: The small top body of ministers that really decides, and its committees.

The Prime Minister and the ministers of Cabinet rank only (not Ministers of State or Deputy Ministers)
Extra-constitutional (not in the Constitution); set up by the Prime Minister under the Rules of Business (government's working rules)
6 of the 8. The PM does not chair the Accommodation Committee or the Parliamentary Affairs Committee
The Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs (the most powerful committee)
Works directly under the Prime Minister; has 3 wings: Civil, Military and Intelligence
T.V. Somanathan — in office since 30 Aug 2024; term extended to 30 Aug 2027 (as of Nov 2026)

blocks.title: Cabinet in the Constitution
items: The original Constitution did not use the word 'Cabinet' anywhere — not even in Art 74 or 75 (they say 'Council of Ministers').
The 44th Amendment (1978) put the word 'Cabinet' into Art 352 (National Emergency). It is the ONLY Article that uses it.
Meaning given in Article 352: 'Cabinet' means the Prime Minister and the other ministers of Cabinet rank appointed under Article 75.
Why it was added: in 1975 the Emergency was declared on the PM's advice alone. Now the President can declare a National Emergency only on the WRITTEN advice of the whole Cabinet, not of the PM alone.

blocks.title: Role of the Cabinet (Laxmikanth)
items: Highest decision-making authority of the system.
Chief policy-making body of the Central government.
Supreme executive authority, and the chief coordinator of the Central administration.
Advisory body to the President — the President must act on its advice.
Chief crisis manager — handles all emergencies.
Handles all major legislative and financial matters.
Controls higher appointments, such as constitutional authorities and senior secretaries.
Handles foreign policy and foreign affairs.

blocks.text: Principle behind Cabinet government: it is the method of parliamentary democracy that makes the whole government jointly ('collectively') responsible to the Lok Sabha, and through it to the people.
For the table comparing the Council of Ministers and the Cabinet, collective responsibility, and ministers from either House, see the Council of Ministers card.

items: An informal small group around the PM, not provided in the Constitution (extra-constitutional) — 'a circle within a circle'.
Members: the PM and a few trusted colleagues. It can also include outsiders, such as friends and family members.
It is the real centre of power: decisions are 'cooked' (made) here first and then placed before the Cabinet only for formal approval.
Every Indian PM has had such an inner group. Under Indira Gandhi it came to be called the 'Kitchen Cabinet' and was very powerful.
Also exists in USA and Britain.

blocks.title: Merits vs demerits
head: Aspect
Merits
Demerits
rows: Being small, it is efficient; it can meet often and decide fast
Helps PM keep important decisions secret
Lowers authority and status of the Cabinet
Lets outsiders influence government, bypassing the legal process

items: Extra-constitutional: they are NOT mentioned in the Constitution. The Rules of Business (the government's own working rules) provide for them.

Two types: standing (permanent) and ad hoc (temporary). An ad hoc committee is formed for a special problem and closed after the work is done — for example, the Emergency Committee of 1962 set up after the Chinese attack.
The Prime Minister sets them up as needed, so their number, names and members keep changing over time.
Members are usually only Cabinet ministers. Ministers below Cabinet rank may sometimes be members or attend as special invitees (invited to attend).
Include the minister in charge of the subject plus other senior ministers.
Mostly the PM chairs them; sometimes another senior Cabinet minister does. Rule: if the PM is a member of a committee, the PM always chairs it.
They do not just prepare proposals for the Cabinet — they also take decisions. Their decisions need no separate approval (ratification) by the full Cabinet, but the Cabinet can review them.
Purpose: to reduce the Cabinet's workload, to study issues in depth, and to improve coordination by dividing work and delegating it.
Temporary (ad hoc) bodies formed for specific urgent issues. The ministers heading the ministries concerned are members.
Some GoMs, called Empowered GoMs (EGoMs), can take decisions on behalf of the Cabinet; the others can only make recommendations.
They are closed once their advice is finalised — they are not permanent.
An effective tool for coordination among ministries.
blocks.title: Groups of Ministers (GoMs)
2nd Administrative Reforms Commission (2005–09, chair Veerappa Moily)
items: Too many GoMs were formed, so many could not meet regularly. This caused delays on major issues.
It recommended using GoMs selectively — each with a clear task (mandate), power to decide on behalf of the Cabinet, and a fixed time limit.

blocks.title: Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs
items: The Ministry works under the overall direction of the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs.
The Minister of Parliamentary Affairs nominates MPs to committees, councils, boards and commissions set up by Central ministries.

blocks.title: Cabinet Secretariat
items: Works under the direct charge of the Prime Minister (NOT under the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs).
Three wings: Civil, Military, Intelligence.
Prepares the agenda of Cabinet meetings, records the decisions taken, and checks that they are carried out.
Gives secretarial help to Cabinet committees.
Administers the Allocation of Business Rules and the Transaction of Business Rules. It also coordinates between ministries and settles their disputes, through Committees of Secretaries.
Does NOT allocate funds to ministries — that is the Finance Ministry's job.

blocks.title: Cabinet Secretary
items: Head of the Cabinet Secretariat; senior-most civil servant (usually an IAS officer); ex-officio chairman of the Civil Services Board.
No fixed term is laid down; the government can extend the term.
Current Cabinet Secretary: Dr T.V. Somanathan. He took charge on 30 Aug 2024, succeeding Rajiv Gauba. His term was extended by one year, to 30 Aug 2027 (as of Nov 2026).
Hung House: no single party has a clear majority in Lok Sabha.
Coalition: two or more parties share government. It need not follow a hung result — pre-poll allies can share power even when one party has a majority.
The partner parties agree on a common programme. Cabinet decisions are taken by consensus (general agreement), and collective responsibility still applies to all ministers.
The Steering Committee or Coordination Committee of the partner parties acts like a 'Super-Cabinet' and weakens the real Cabinet.
The PM must consult the partner parties. Critics call the partner leaders 'Super Prime Ministers'.
Small partner parties may act as 'King-makers' (deciding who forms the government).
Coalitions lead to very large ministries: the Vajpayee ministry (1999) had more than 70 ministers and was called the 'Jumbo Ministry'.
The word 'Cabinet' appears only in Article 352, added by the 44th Amendment (1978). It was never in the original Article 74.
Cabinet committees and the kitchen cabinet are both extra-constitutional. The Rules of Business (not the Constitution) provide for the committees.
Committee decisions take effect without approval by the full Cabinet, but the Cabinet can review them.
The Cabinet Secretariat works under the PM, not under the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs. It does not allocate money to ministries.
Cabinet Secretariat wings: Civil, Military, Intelligence.
'Super Cabinet' means the Political Affairs Committee. In coalition governments, the Steering or Coordination Committee is also called a 'Super-Cabinet'.
The PM does NOT chair the Parliamentary Affairs Committee (chair: Rajnath Singh) or the Accommodation Committee (chair: Amit Shah) (as of Nov 2026).
Bagehot called the Cabinet 'a hyphen that joins, a buckle that binds'. Ramsay Muir spoke of the 'Dictatorship of the Cabinet'. Jennings called it 'the core of the British Constitutional System'.
